subject: Creativity
title: Failure Kills Creativity: Why Getting It Wrong Gets It Right
description: A short lesson to help you apply Failure Kills Creativity: Why Getting It Wrong Gets It Right.

hook.text: WD-40 got its name because it was the 40th attempt. The first 39 were failures.

buildup.text: The myth says failure discourages creativity. But research shows that creators who experience early failure produce.

discovery.text: Failure forces adaptation — new approaches, new combinations, new perspectives. Success encourages repetition.

twist.text: Dean Keith Simonton found that the most creative scientists have the MOST failures — because they attempt the most.

climax.text: Pixar's Ed Catmull says: 'Every Pixar movie sucks at first.' The creative process IS the process of making bad things.

punchline.text: Failure doesn't kill creativity. Fear of failure does.

quiz.question: What does Dean Keith Simonton's research show about creative scientists?
options: The most creative scientists have the MOST failures because they attempt the most experiments

details.summary: Failure does not kill creativity; it is an essential component of the creative process. Every successful innovation is preceded by numerous failures that provide the information needed to find what works. Fear of failure, not failure itself, is what actually kills creative output.
details.whyItMatters: Reframing failure as information rather than defeat removes the biggest psychological barrier to creative risk-taking. Organizations and individuals who embrace failure produce more innovation.
takeaways: Failure provides essential information about what does not work
Fear of failure is more damaging to creativity than failure itself
Edison's 1,000 failed experiments informed his eventual success

faq.question: How do you learn from creative failure?
faq.answer: Analyze what specifically did not work and why. Distinguish between failures of execution and failures of concept. Use each failure to refine your approach. The key is structured reflection rather than simply trying again without adjustment.

faq.question: How do organizations create cultures that accept failure?
faq.answer: By rewarding effort and learning rather than only outcomes. Leaders must model vulnerability by sharing their own failures. Psychological safety, where people feel safe taking risks, is the foundation of creative organizational culture.
